fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so it's a fair question, and honestly the answer is a little less dramatic than people expect. I'd actually already accepted the Princeton position when I went to OpenAI. The year there was really more like a postdoc for me, a chance to see what industrial research looked like before I started a lab of my own. So it wasn't so much a choice between the two as it was the plan all along, and OpenAI happened to be an amazing detour.

That said, there were real reasons I wanted to be in academia. Coming out of my PhD, the thing I cared most about was language in the context of agents: systems that read instructions and then act in some environment, text games, that kind of thing. In 2017 that was pretty far from what most industry labs were prioritizing. Being a professor means I get to pick problems because I think they matter in five or ten years, not because they fit this quarter's roadmap. And I get to be a little wrong for a while without anyone asking me to justify it.

The other piece is students. I genuinely love the process of taking someone who's smart but hasn't done research before and watching them find their own taste. That compounds in a way that's hard to replicate anywhere else. A lot of what my group has done since, on agents and benchmarks and so on, came from students pushing in directions I wouldn't have on my own.

And look, in hindsight, with what OpenAI became, people assume I must have regrets. I don't, really. I got to be part of the first GPT paper, I learned a ton from Alec and Ilya, and then I got to go build something that's mine. I think I ended up with the best of both.

r001.rationale: The response clearly emphasizes academic freedom to choose problems based on long-term importance rather than an industry roadmap, supporting exploration of multiple research directions as the main reason for choosing Princeton.

opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it wasn't a hard decision at the time, though in hindsight people assume it must have been. When I was at OpenAI, it was still a small research lab. GPT was one project among many, and nobody, including us, knew it would become what it became. We thought it was a neat result: pre-train a language model on a lot of unlabeled text, fine-tune it, and get nice gains across a bunch of benchmarks. It was exciting, but it didn't feel like the moment where you think, "I have to stay here, this is going to change the world."

I'd always wanted to be in academia. Even during my PhD I knew I liked the freedom to pick problems that weren't tied to any one product or agenda. And I really enjoy working with students. Watching someone come in as a first-year who's unsure of themselves and leave five years later with their own research voice is one of the most rewarding parts of the job. You don't quite get that in an industry lab.

Princeton was a great fit. It's a place that values deep, foundational work, the department was growing in machine learning and NLP, and I'd have room to build a group around questions I cared about, like language and agents, getting models to act in the world and not just predict text.

Of course, the field has changed dramatically since then. Scale became a big part of the story, and that's harder to pursue at a university. But I think academia still has a really important role: asking the questions industry isn't incentivized to ask, doing careful evaluation, thinking about where these systems fail, and training the next generation of researchers. So I don't really see it as choosing one over the other. They're different vantage points on the same problems, and I've been lucky to stay connected to both.

r001.rationale: The response clearly presents academic freedom to choose problems across areas and build a research group around questions of interest as a central reason for choosing Princeton over OpenAI.

fable-5.text:
Well, it's funny because at the time, that didn't seem like such a strange decision as it might look in retrospect. This was 2018, and OpenAI was a very different place back then — it was still a nonprofit, a fairly small research lab, and honestly nobody knew that language models were going to become what they became. I had just finished working on the GPT project, and it was exciting, but it wasn't obvious that scaling that recipe was going to change the world.

For me, it really came down to a few things. First, I'd always wanted to be an academic — that was the plan going through my PhD at MIT. I love the freedom of being able to pick my own problems and chase ideas that might not pay off for five or ten years, without needing to justify them against an organization's roadmap. And second, I genuinely enjoy working with students. There's something special about taking someone who's just starting out in research and watching them grow into an independent thinker — that mentorship aspect is something you really only get in academia.

The other piece was intellectual. I was very interested in the intersection of language and decision-making — agents that could read and then act in the world, grounding language in environments — and at the time, that wasn't really the central focus anywhere in industry. Academia felt like the right place to build a group around those questions. And I'd like to think that bet aged reasonably well, because a lot of that agenda — language agents, using text to guide behavior — has now become central to the field. So I don't regret it, even if people occasionally remind me what the counterfactual equity package might have looked like.

r001.rationale: The response clearly cites academic freedom to pick his own problems and pursue ideas with uncertain payoffs, which communicates the opportunity to explore multiple research directions as a primary reason for choosing Princeton.

opus-5.text:
Honestly, part of it was timing. When I finished at OpenAI, the thing we'd done with GPT was exciting but it wasn't at all obvious that this was going to be *the* paradigm — it looked like one promising direction among several. So the choice didn't feel like "industry versus academia at the frontier" the way it would today. It felt more like: what kind of problems do I want to spend the next decade on, and what environment lets me chase the ones that are weird?

And the academic environment is unusually good for weird. At a lab, even a great one, there's a direction, and your work has to serve it — which is the right way to run a lab, but it means a lot of questions get deprioritized not because they're uninteresting but because they're not on the critical path. I was interested in things like how agents actually interact with the world, grounding language in environments, how you evaluate whether a system understands anything at all. Some of that has become very central now, but at the time it was off to the side. Princeton lets me just go do it.

The other piece, which I think people underrate until they've done it, is students. You get to work with people who are at the stage where they'll argue with you about fundamentals, who haven't yet learned which questions you're not supposed to ask. I've had my mind changed by first-year PhD students more than once. That's a very different intellectual diet than being surrounded by extremely competent people all pushing in the same direction.

I won't pretend there's no cost. Compute is the obvious one — there are experiments I simply can't run, and that gap has gotten wider, not narrower. You have to be strategic about picking problems where you're not just doing a smaller, worse version of what a frontier lab is doing. But I'd rather be asking a question nobody's asking with limited resources than be the fiftieth person on a problem that's already well-staffed.

r001.rationale: The response explains that Princeton offered freedom to pursue varied, unconventional research questions—such as agents, grounding, and evaluation—rather than follow a lab’s established direction, presenting this flexibility as the central reason for leaving OpenAI.

sonnet-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd say it wasn't a choice between the two so much as a question of what I wanted to spend my time on. My time at OpenAI was a great experience. It was a small, intense group, and the first GPT work came out of it. But I'd always seen myself as an academic. What I enjoy most is picking a problem I find interesting, working on it with students over a long stretch, and following where it goes, even when it isn't the obvious thing to scale up right now.

Being a professor also means I get to work with students as they develop their own taste and ideas, and that's the part I find most rewarding. Some of the questions I care about, like how language models can act, plan, and interact with the world instead of just predicting text, benefit from that open-ended exploration. You don't always have to justify a direction by its near-term payoff.

I also think academia has an important role right now. A lot of the large-scale work happens in industry, but there's still a lot to do in understanding why these systems work, where they break, and how to make them more reliable. Having people who can step back and ask those questions feels valuable to me. So it was less about leaving something behind and more about being in the place where I could do the work I find most meaningful.

r001.rationale: The response presents academic, open-ended exploration—pursuing interesting problems with students and following questions without near-term payoff—as the main reason for choosing Princeton over OpenAI, which conveys the opportunity to explore varied research directions.
